judgements.justification: A's area chair added a novelty objection, but the reject matched A's scores (4, 4, 4, 5); B's area chair shared the detractor's doubts and gave no reading of its own that lifted the paper.

B's area chair accepted 'in particular because there is potential for RBNs to be an important model', a forecast the thin experiments do not show and A never made; B's own Reviewer_1oXa doubted any important application.
The rebuttal lifted A's Reviewer_c2bx only 'a bit', to 4, and changed no recommendation; no B score moved, so the response did not drive the split.
B's four reviews ran 312 to 396 words and Reviewer_VzMU praised experiments and limitations that are not there, while three A reviews ran 530 to 1,578 words and examined the music figures.

Only A found the conceded Chomsky-normal-form gap, the Bach tree that misses the expert's large-scale grouping, the authors' own expert annotation and the missing hidden-tree-Markov-model work, and these fed A's reject.

Six of eight reviewers doubted the same thin evidence (synthetic data drawn from an RBN, one corpus of 24 major preludes); A made it decisive, while B's positive reviewers valued the formalism and excused it.
No reviewer on either committee changed a score after reading the other reviewers.

B's Reviewer_1oXa rated 8 while writing 'some much simpler method could also have done this' and doubting any important application; A's Reviewer_k7kf called the paper a 'Good contribution' yet rated 4.
A's one unsure reviewer, Reviewer_k7kf (confidence 1), rated 4, not a borderline placeholder, and A's other reviewers gave confident, specific verdicts.
B's area chair agreed with its outlying detractor Reviewer_K4dB but accepted against that view; A's area chair followed unanimous scores.

The committees' written verdicts differ in substance (A's reviews name decisive evaluation failures), so the gap is weighting and scrutiny, not calibration of similar verdicts; single-review mismatches fall under R08.
Neither committee was unanimous at an accept level; B's scores spread from 5 to 8.
No B score rose after the rebuttal, and A's one small rise rested on clarification, not new unverified results.
B's meta-review carried Reviewer_K4dB's overclaiming concern forward, and A's meta-review cited its reviewers' scores.

B's Reviewer_VzMU (6) wrote that the music experiments 'demonstrate the effectiveness' and that limitations 'are discussed', both checked as incorrect: no music baseline, no limitations section, and a caption that reports failure.
The authors' concessions (upper tree levels 'have almost nothing in common', pitch counting gives the same profile) went to A, which rejected; B heard no comparable admission.
No objection or score change came after the response period without an author reply.
The two committees' scores differ (4, 4, 4, 5 against 7, 8, 6, 5), so the split is not a tier cut-off applied to near-identical reviews.
B's area chair weighed its detractor's concern explicitly, and A's area chair followed reviewers who agreed; no expert verdict was passed over.
Neither committee's scores moved materially after the rebuttal; A's concerns were about evaluation scope, and B's were mostly already positive.
Neither committee has an outlying score; A's ratings are tight and B's spread evenly from 5 to 8.
No outlying reviewer stood unrevised against an answered rebuttal; Reviewer_k7kf and Reviewer_VzMU were silent but not outliers.
No area chair set aside a detractor as unreliable; B's area chair agreed with its detractor.
A's Reviewer_k7kf called music 'a very narrow domain', but this concerns the breadth of the evaluation that all A reviewers questioned, not audience or venue fit.
A's area chair added an own novelty view but did not misreport the reviewers' positions or the rebuttal; B's meta-review reports K4dB's concern accurately.
Most reviewers on both committees replied to the response; only one reviewer per committee stayed silent.
No B reviewer had confidence below 3 or said they could not verify the results.
Neither committee split evenly; A was uniformly below threshold and B three to one above.
The authors' concessions to A answered objections only A raised; the notes show no conflicting results or accounts across the two responses.
No reviewer's novelty verdict rested on a shown wrong account of prior work; the closely related latent vector grammars surfaced only after acceptance, and A's area chair named no prior work.

added.name: Higher tier given with no stated grounds
added.definition: One committee's recommendation reached a higher tier than its scores or its own meta-review supported, and nothing in its record argued for that tier, so part of the split reflects an unexplained tier assignment, not the reviews.
added.justification: R18 needs near-identical scores and R01 needs the area chair's own reading to drive the tier; here B's spotlight rests on a 6.5 mean with a 5, under a meta-review that shared the detractor's concerns and said only that the work 'may be enough for justifying publication'.

reasoning: The committees saw the same thin evidence and weighted it oppositely (R06): A's longer, more searching reviews found failures only they raised (R04, R05), while B's positive reviewers praised or excused the experiments, one with a misreading of the paper (R15) and one with an 8 above its own text (R08). B's area chair accepted on a forecast that RBNs could become important (R02). The spotlight itself has no argued basis: B's meta-review is lukewarm and its mean is 6.5, and no existing reason names an unexplained tier, so R31 was added. The rebuttal, discussion and outlier reasons do not apply.
